The Independent National Electoral Commission has dismissed as false claims that the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System can be remotely logged out before the end of voting, assuring Nigerians that only polling officials operating the devices have the authority to log in or out. The commission said a viral video circulating on Instagram, which alleged that voters could be logged out of the BVAS before the close of voting, was fabricated and misleading. INEC made the clarification in a statement posted on its official X handle on Monday, following the circulation of the video. “For the avoidance of doubt, the commission wishes to clarify the operational procedures of the BVAS and the process for uploading polling unit results to the INEC Result Viewing Portal,” it said. The commission explained that each polling unit was assigned unique login credentials, which were issued to presiding officers on the eve of an election. According to INEC, the credentials enable presiding officers to access the BVAS for voter accreditation on election day and subsequently upload polling unit result sheets after voting. “The claim that the BVAS can be remotely logged out before the conclusion of accreditation and voting is false,” the commission stated. It added, “Only the poll official operating the device has the authority to log in or log out of the BVAS, whether during voter accreditation or the result upload process. There is no provision for remote log-out by any external individual or authority.” INEC also dismissed claims that election results uploaded offline could be lost, explaining that it had upgraded the IReV application following challenges experienced during the 2023 general elections. The commission said the upgrade introduced an offline upload capability to enable presiding officers in areas with poor or no network coverage to upload polling unit result sheets in the presence of stakeholders. It recalled that during the 2023 elections, some polling officials were held hostage at their polling units because they could not upload results due to poor or unavailable network connectivity. Explaining how the offline feature works, INEC said, “The uploaded result sheet remains securely stored on the BVAS pending successful transmission.” It added that once polling officials moved from their polling units to ward collation centres and their devices regained internet connectivity, the results would automatically be transmitted to the IReV portal without further manual intervention. INEC urged members of the public to disregard the viral video and avoid creating or circulating unverified information. It advised Nigerians to rely on its official communication channels for accurate information, reaffirming its commitment to conducting free, fair and credible elections. Meanwhile, experts have raised concerns over the handling of voters’ personal data by INEC, warning that inadequate transparency and data protection could expose Nigeria’s 2027 general elections to manipulation. The experts, who spoke at a roundtable on voter privacy and data transparency in Nigeria’s electioneering process in Abuja on Monday, urged INEC to disclose how it collects, stores, processes and shares voters’ information with third-party technology providers. Co-founder of the Digital Rights Lawyers Initiative, Olumide Babalola, said electoral bodies had failed to meet the transparency requirements stipulated in the Nigeria Data Protection Act, despite handling critical national data and sensitive personal data. Babalola said Nigerians deserved to know how their personal information was managed, particularly as technology increasingly shaped the electoral process. He said, “The Nigerian Data Protection Act provides for whoever handles personal data, either as a business concern or for whatever purpose, to be transparent in their use, in their sharing, in the processing generally. Whatever they do with data, the law requires them to be transparent. “INEC and the other 36 electoral commissions handle critical national data. They also handle sensitive personal data. But what we have discovered over time is that they are not transparent in the use of that.” Tinubu tightens security, 128 police chiefs redeployed 2027: Osun Senator Fadahunsi begins re-election campaign One dies as herders clash with campaign convoy in Jigawa He identified the absence of accessible information on electoral technology providers, data storage systems, privacy policies and data protection officers as major gaps requiring urgent attention. According to him, INEC operates multiple websites, some of which are incomplete, making it difficult for citizens to identify its official platform and access information about its data management practices. He also questioned the level of disclosure surrounding the technology vendors responsible for platforms such as the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and the INEC Result Viewing Portal. Babalola said, “I am a lawyer. I do not know who runs BVAS. Where is the data stored? Where is the server? I mean, the bidding process, the security infrastructure. We do not have all this. “We should be able to know the vendors handling data, INEC’s digital platforms. They are very important. We should be able to know them and their antecedents.” He disclosed that the organisation had filed a suit against INEC over alleged lapses in data transparency, but that the commission had yet to respond to the case. He added that a Freedom of Information request to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission indicated that INEC had been compliant with data protection requirements in only one year covered by the inquiry. The lawyer said the organisation’s research also found that only about two state electoral commissions had websites, while others relied on websites belonging to state government agencies. He argued that such arrangements raised questions about their institutional independence and ability to provide voters with adequate information about their data protection practices. Babalola further called on INEC to explain the recent cases involving alleged AI-generated voter registration details and the reported unauthorised access to the voter information of actor Emeka Ike. He said Nigerians deserved to know what happened to those implicated in the incidents and whether they had been prosecuted. Earlier, a representative of Luminate, Adegboye Adegoke, said the growing use of technology in elections had made the protection and governance of electoral data increasingly important. He said the introduction of technology into voter registration, accreditation and other electoral processes had created new vulnerabilities that could be exploited if the information collected by electoral institutions was not properly secured. Adegoke said, “Data is very powerful. We are also in the age of artificial intelligence, where people can use AI to manipulate data. “So, when an institution has such amounts of data or sensitive data, there are a lot of questions that they need to answer in terms of how they manage that data and how they ensure fairness to all the candidates and political parties in the election.” He warned that individuals with access to electoral databases could manipulate information and undermine the credibility of elections. He added that transparency alone was insufficient without adequate privacy safeguards and security measures to prevent unauthorised access and manipulation. Also speaking, the Executive Director of Digital Africa Research and Safety Lab, Rosemary Ajayi, stressed that it was mandatory for INEC to handle voters’ information with utmost safety ahead of the 2027 elections. She identified the reported access to actor Emeka Ike’s voter information by a serving government official and allegations surrounding AI-generated voter details as issues requiring greater scrutiny. Ajayi said citizens were also considering different monitoring tools, including drones and body cameras, to document electoral activities as they increasingly explored ways to monitor the electoral process and protect their votes. The experts said improving data transparency, strengthening privacy safeguards and providing Nigerians with adequate information about electoral technology would be essential to building public confidence ahead of the 2027 general elections.
